documents: Jiang, Shan, Guo, Zhao, Wang & Zhao (2022), Tropical tropopause in Tibet: Insights from ground-based GNSS and space-based radio occultation observations, Meteorological Applications 29:e2090, published PDF (16 pp.)

entry.evidence: Our aim is to address the problems of insufficient short-term single observation data in Tibet

sequences.source_document: Jiang et al. 2022, Meteorological Applications 29:e2090 (published PDF)

steps.action: States the aim: overcome sparse radiosonde and RO coverage in Tibet by testing whether ground-based GNSS, alone and combined with RO, can retrieve and monitor the tropopause.
steps.quote: to verify the suitability of tropopause research based on [...]

steps.action: Assembles daily GAMIT ZTD from 49 Tibetan GNSS stations (2017-2019), NCEP/DOE, ERA5 and JRA55 reanalysis profiles, and COSMIC and GRACE RO wetPrf profiles (948 and 204 events).
steps.quote: We obtained daily zenith total delay (ZTD) data from 49 GNSS stations (Figure 1) in Tibet from 2017 to 2019 through GAMIT

steps.action: Adopts the published RO refractivity tropopause method (wavelet covariance transform, a = 25 km, Lewis 2009 / ROPP) with a 150 hPa split between LRT1 and LRT2.
steps.quote: The RO tropopause height was determined directly from the refractivity profiles using covariance transforms

steps.action: Builds the GNSS inversion on Astudillo et al. (2020): fits an exponential refractivity profile to ERA5-derived N, adds the Saastamoinen ZHD above the tropopause, and takes the height that minimizes the ZTD residual as TPH(GNSS).
steps.quote: Compared with the method of Astudillo et al. (2020), we consider the influence of ZHD above the tropopause.

steps.action: Checks the premises against 2017 radiosondes at Lhasa, Qamdo and Nagqu: compares P, T and e from three reanalyses (ERA5 chosen), tests ERA5 P and N profile errors against literature thresholds (2.5 hPa, 4 N), and shows GNSS+ERA5 ZTD profiles beat ERA5 alone below 10 km at LHAZ.
steps.quote: confirm that ERA5 has better applicability in Tibet compared with JRA55 and NCEP/DOE

steps.action: Inverts TPH(GNSS) for the 49 stations over 2017-2019 and interprets it as the second (tropical) tropopause.
steps.quote: The TPH(GNSS) obtained based on ground-based GNSS combined with reanalysis data inversion represents the second tropopause.

steps.action: Checks the plausibility of TPH(GNSS) patterns (negative latitude dependence in February, unimodal seasonal cycle at LHAZ with 0.8 km amplitude) against the published seasonal cycle.
steps.quote: which is consistent with the results of Zhou et al. (2010)

steps.action: Compares 19,548 TPH(GNSS) values with LRT2 from ERA5 temperature profiles: bias 0.17 km, RMS 0.89 km, over 90% within 2 km (Table 4).
steps.quote: the difference between TPH(GNSS) and LRT2 (ERA5) was within 2 km in more than 90% of the cases

steps.action: Attributes the larger winter-spring differences at LHAZ (Figure 6) to ERA5 temperature biases in the reference, not to the GNSS method.
steps.quote: which may be because the ERA5 mean temperature biases have a small

steps.action: Because RO events in Tibet are too few per day (Figure 7), accumulates RO over one month to get even spatial coverage, and uses the refractivity tropopause rather than the RO LRT product.
steps.quote: we obtained a denser spatial resolution of sampling points that provided even coverage across Tibet

steps.action: Compares TPH(RO) from COSMIC and GRACE with LRT2(ERA5) and, for colocated events (<2 degrees, <3 h), with TPH(GNSS); RMS about 1.3 km vs ERA5 and 1.19/1.31 km vs GNSS (Table 5).
steps.quote: [...] , we determined the relative accuracies of TPH(RO) and LRT2(ERA5) using 110 COSMIC and 55 GRACE occultation events

steps.action: Concludes that TPH(RO) and TPH(GNSS) are at the same accuracy level and can be combined.
steps.quote: these two technologies can be combined to analyse the tropopause in Tibet

steps.action: Maps seasonal mean tropopause heights from combined GNSS and RO (2017-2019), finding a south-to-north decrease and a tropopause break at 30-34 N (Figure 9).
steps.quote: Figure 9 shows seasonal average tropopause heights in the region and reveals a zonal distribution

steps.action: Compares the regional tropopause break with the hemispheric average break latitude reported by Hoinka (1999).
steps.quote: which is slightly narrower than the average

steps.action: Explains the seasonal changes with published mechanisms (solar heating and convection, South Asian monsoon, latent heat release), citing other groups.
steps.quote: the outbreak of the South Asian summer monsoon, which enhances deep convection

steps.action: Removes the seasonal cycle from monthly combined tropopause heights and reports a slight downward trend for 2017-2019 (Figure 10).
steps.quote: the tropopause height fluctuates around 0 but shows a slight downward trend

steps.action: Matches the anomaly series to Tibet climate bulletins: annual temperature decline, warm winter 2017, cold snowy winter 2019, summer 2019 precipitation.
steps.quote: a downward trend that is consistent with the change in the tropopause

steps.action: Keeps the headline claim that ground-based GNSS, combined with RO, can detect and monitor the regional tropopause.
steps.quote: our results confirm that GNSS data can be used to detect the height of the tropopause

tree.answer: Tropopause height over Tibet: a known phenomenon, poorly sampled
No; inferred from GNSS ZTD through an ERA5 refractivity model
Characterize a GNSS retrieval method and describe regional patterns
No rival hypotheses; alternative data sources (reanalyses, RO, radiosonde) compared
Conditions found: archived GNSS, reanalysis and RO data, 2017-2019
Agreement with ERA5 LRT2 (RMS 0.89 km) and RO (RMS about 1.25 km)
Kept: method usable, accuracy comparable to RO

end.claim: Ground-based GNSS ZTD combined with ERA5 retrieves the second tropopause in Tibet within 2 km of ERA5 LRT2 in over 90% of cases and with accuracy comparable to RO (RMS about 1.25 km), so GNSS and RO can be combined for regional tropopause monitoring.

decisive_move.sentence: The inversion that fits an ERA5 refractivity profile to station ZTD, with ZHD above the tropopause added, produces TPH(GNSS); without it there is no GNSS tropopause to validate or combine with RO.

gates.evidence: Data are archived GNSS, reanalysis and RO products, collected without a hypothesis directing acquisition. The method could have failed against ERA5 LRT2 and RO, but the acceptance criterion ('within 2 km in more than 90% of cases', 'same accuracy level') is stated only after the results, and ERA5 enters both the retrieval and the reference. The reanalysis thresholds (2.5 hPa, 4 N) come from earlier literature, but the paper does not say any analysis or threshold was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Exponential model of atmospheric radio refractivity with height (Bean & Thayer 1959, Proceedings of the IRE)
Wavelet covariance transform for detecting step changes in signals (Gamage & Hagelberg 1993)
Thomson (1946) on the Antoine vapor-pressure equation, cited for the definition of tropospheric delay

novelty_claims.quote: there are few studies on the use of ground-based GNSS to study the tropopause
an improved method has been developed for the inversion of the tropical tropopause
Compared with the method of Astudillo et al. (2020), we consider the influence of ZHD above the tropopause.

limits:
No review file or earlier version was supplied, so only the final_paper sequence is coded.

Reference not independent: ERA5 supplies the refractivity and pressure profiles in the GNSS retrieval and is also the main validation reference (LRT2(ERA5)). The ERA5 comparison is therefore only partly independent, and the effect of this shared input is not assessed.

Narrow premise checks: the radiosonde checks cover only three stations in 2017. The ZTD-profile test covers one station (LHAZ, 2017), and the improvement is small (1.88 vs 1.78 cm mean RMS).

Unquantified modification: the effect of adding ZHD above the tropopause (the stated improvement over Astudillo et al.) is never quantified against the original method.

Inconsistent RMS: the GNSS-ERA5 RMS is 0.89 km on p. 9 but ±0.87 km in the Conclusions (p. 14).

Discrepancy not tested: the winter discrepancy is attributed to ERA5 temperature bias, citing Betts et al. 2019 for the Canadian prairies, without a test in Tibet (protective move).

Sub-claims at other statuses:
- Latitude-zoned distribution, unimodal seasonal cycle and 30-34 N break: regularity_in_range (Tibet, 2017-2019).
- Slight downward trend and its links to warm or cold winters and precipitation: at most best_explanation. These rest on three years, no significance test or uncertainty, and post hoc qualitative matching to climate bulletins, with mechanisms cited rather than tested.

Unexplained choices: the RO colocation criteria (<2 degrees, <3 h) and the a = 25 km wavelet scale are adopted without stated alternatives.

Data not public: GNSS data are available only on request.

Inference: the Thomson (1946) citation for tropospheric delay appears to be a mis-citation.

disagreements.support: Argues that the delay above the tropopause (about 20%) is not negligible and adds a Saastamoinen ZHD term, but reports no comparison with the original method.

disagreements.target: Hoinka (1999) average 30-45 N tropopause break for the northern hemisphere
disagreements.support: Combined GNSS and RO seasonal maps place the break over Tibet at 30-34 N, narrower than the hemispheric average.
disagreements.quote: which is slightly narrower than the average

disagreements.target: Temperature-profile (WMO lapse-rate) tropopause and the RO LRT product
disagreements.support: Citing Xia et al. (2021) and the hydrostatic and ideal-gas assumptions of RO temperature retrieval, the paper uses the refractivity tropopause instead.
disagreements.quote: it is somewhat difficult to identify the tropopause height

disagreements.target: ERA5 LRT2 as a reference in winter and spring (ERA5 temperature biases, Betts et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: Larger winter-spring differences at LHAZ are attributed to seasonal ERA5 temperature bias.
